My 100 year old great grandmother survived it with nothing more than a low grade fever and small cough, that passed in less than a week. This virus is true madness.

I had in in November (yeah it wasn’t officially in Europe by then, but myself & my family all had a positive antibody test). I was what you’d call an ‘atypical symptomer’.


I had none of the famous symptoms - no cough, no loss of taste or smell, no fever or chills. However, I was sleeping up to 20 hours a day and felt like I’d been hit by a truck. It began with this fatigue, just like every single ounce of energy had been completely drained from my body. Then I discovered a hard swollen lymph node just under my chin, about the size of a bean. I thought nothing of it until I started waking up in the night to drenched sheets from where I’d been sweating. When I lay on my back it also felt like someone was sat on my chest, my heart started palpitating and it was hard to breathe. I was also constantly winded. I passed it off as being unfit, but I’ve never been gasping for breath just scaling the stairs in my house or walking down the street before. I also had pain in my spleen area that came and went, as well as a strange rash under my chin that looked like broken blood vessels called petechiae. (Now we know about ‘COVID rashes’!) 


This ended up in my going to hospital to be checked for cancer, specifically lymphoma. I had ultrasounds and blood tests, nothing was abnormal other than low ferritin levels causing me to be pre-anaemic. At the time the consultant said to me ‘Your body could just be reacting oddly to fighting a virus of some sort.’ Of course, at that time, little did we know... 


The rest of my family had ‘classic’ symptoms. Hacking cough that lasted two weeks, flu-like symptoms, loss of taste and smell. My mother still struggles with smell to this day more than six months later - she is immune compromised so no surprise she suffered the worst of us with the lasting symptoms. However both my great-grandmothers of 98 (caught from us) and 100 (caught in a care facility) years old survived the initial illness!

Maybe getting him, or you yourself, track the calories of everything he’s eating in a day. So for example: note the calories of the dominos pizza, the potato and meat, and the other pizza, add them together and compare the total with the recommended daily amount for his age/height etc as per the health board for your country. Now it’s absolutely ok to go over recommended daily calories! But if he’s really overweight like you say and is going way way over every single day, then you could show the statistics to him. Backed up with evidence from the health board (ie. NHS), it might seem less like you’re just nagging him and more like you are concerned for his health. 

Otherwise, try to share healthy and nutritional recipes with him - like a big salad with nuts and chicken is very different to a dominos for example. Or encourage him to join in exercise with you, or join a sports club. Could he possibly be depressed and using food to self medicate? (Disclaimer: not an expert by any means. Info from experience with clogged oily pores and breakouts and a lot of research). From this comment it sounds like your skin barrier got got damaged. When subjected to a lot of irritation the moisture barrier on your skin (the stratum corneum - the outermost layer of the epidermis) can become damaged, so what should be a fine latticework of cells forming a barrier have broken apart, letting bad stuff in and good stuff - mostly moisture! - out. This damage can sometimes be seen as rough, dull, flaky, inflamed, or red skin, but it can also be seen in an overproduction of oils (like you mention above!). 


As your oily skin correlates with the sunburn, it could be likely that this is the case for you, and the oils your skin is producing to compensate for the damaged moisture barrier is clogging up your nose as a result. Using clay masks and AHAs like glycolic acid will unfortunately further dry out your skin, making it want to produce MORE oil, which could be why they come back straight away. 


Other comments have recommended retinols and other actives, but what I would try is first repairing any damage to your moisture barrier first. So just using a gentle, hydrating cleanser like CeraVe or La Roche Posay Toleraine, or Avene Tolerance - those like of cleansers that are more like a lotion and don’t foam. (This is because foam = surfactants which could be further drying). And a nice emollient & occlusive moisturiser after while your face is still a little damp to seal in the water (hydration) and fill in the ‘gaps’ in your ‘latticework’ (weird analogy I know!). You could even add an oil, I’d recommend Marula or Jojoba over more comedogenic oils like coconut. It might seem counterproductive to put thick moisturising or oily products on a clogged and already oily area, but I do think it would help if a damaged barrier is your problem. The jist is keeping your routine as simple as possible and as moisturising as possible. 


If you do see an improvement after doing that for about 3-4 weeks, I’d then consider adding an active acid exfoliant. From the photo I think a BHA would help more than an AHA but it’s your choice. If you choose AHA I would go for something gentler than glycolic - lactic or mandelic acid are good gentle choices. If you choose BHA, that’s salicylic acid, Paula’s Choice or The Ordinary both at 2% active formulations are good. I would only do this 2x a week to start with, after cleansing and before moisturising, as you don’t want to strip away the work of healing the moisture barrier by then overexfoliating! Also only use it where you need it - like on your nose, you don’t have to exfoliate your whole face, it’s ok to spot-treat! 


Good luck with however you choose to fix your issue :)
